what_it_does: Acts as a lightweight emollient and solvent that helps products spread smoothly.
summary_short: Isopropyl myristate is mainly used to make formulas feel silky, light, and easy to spread. It can reduce greasiness in creams, lotions, and sunscreens, but it may be pore-clogging for some acne-prone users.
summary_long:
**Isopropyl myristate is an ester of isopropyl alcohol and myristic acid**. In skincare, it is most often used as an emollient, slip agent, and solvent, helping creams, lotions, sunscreens, and makeup glide more smoothly without feeling heavy or sticky.

It works mostly through **texture and delivery**, not by treating a skin concern directly. Its oily-but-light structure can soften the skin surface, improve spreadability, and help dissolve oil-soluble ingredients. In some formulations, it may also help active ingredients move through the outer skin layer, which is useful in drug delivery but can also make irritation more noticeable if paired with strong actives.

Evidence for isopropyl myristate is strongest around its **formulation role**: it is a well-established cosmetic ingredient for improving feel, slip, and solubility. It is not typically used as a hero ingredient for hydration, anti-aging, acne, or brightening, though it may make a moisturizer feel more cosmetically elegant.

The main drawback is that isopropyl myristate has a reputation for being **comedogenic in some people**, especially in leave-on products used on oily or acne-prone areas. Comedogenicity ratings are imperfect and do not predict everyone’s experience, but users who notice clogged pores from rich creams or oily esters may want to patch-test or avoid it high on the ingredient list.

Irritation is generally uncommon, but sensitivity can happen, particularly when it helps other ingredients penetrate more readily. It often appears alongside emollients, silicones, sunscreens, fragrance, and oil-soluble actives. There are no universal “do not mix” conflicts, but acne-prone or easily irritated skin may prefer simpler formulas when using strong actives like retinoids, exfoliating acids, or benzoyl peroxide.
quick_facts: May clog pores for some users
Common in creams, sunscreens, and makeup
